extraction.name: CT-RATE
extraction.description: CT-RATE is a dataset comprising 25,692 non-contrast 3D chest CT scans from 21,304 unique patients, with each scan accompanied by its corresponding radiology report. The dataset includes over 14.3 million 2D slices reconstructed using various methods, with reports containing impression and findings sections authored by radiologists. Each volume is annotated with 18 abnormalities.
extraction.creator: Ibrahim Ethem Hamamci, Sezgin Er, and collaborators from University of Zurich, ETH Zurich, Istanbul Medipol University, Boston University, and other institutions
extraction.publisher: University of Zurich and Istanbul Medipol University
extraction.rai:dataCollection: CT-RATE comprises 25,692 non-contrast 3D chest CT scans from 21,304 unique patients, with each scan accompanied by its corresponding radiology report. The dataset includes 50,188 reconstructed 3D chest CT volumes (over 14.3 million 2D slices) paired with radiology text reports. Data was collected from electronic health records at a single institution. Multi-abnormality labels were extracted from reports using a finetuned language model, with manual annotation of a small portion of reports to develop an automatic labeler.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The raw data consists of non-contrast 3D chest CT scans and their corresponding radiology text reports from electronic health records. Each 3D volume contains multiple 2D slices (over 14.3 million total slices across the dataset). The reports include impression and findings sections written by radiologists as part of routine clinical practice.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Manual annotation of 1,000 reports for 18 distinct abnormalities by domain experts, followed by automated text classification using a finetuned language model (RadBERT) to extract multi-abnormality labels from radiology reports. For CT-CHAT, over 2.7 million question-answer pairs were generated from CT-RATE using Llama 3.1 7B. Expert evaluation involved three board-certified radiologists who independently rated 150 reports for each model on a scale from 0 to 10 based on predefined clinical criteria.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The finetuned text classification model's precision, recall, and F1 scores were evaluated and detailed in Supplementary Table 2, showing robust classification across abnormalities. For expert evaluation, mean scores from three board-certified radiologists were computed: Radiologist 1 rated CT-CHAT at 3.44, Radiologist 2 at 4.10, and Radiologist 3 at 4.52.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: For expert evaluation, each of 150 reports was independently rated by three board-certified radiologists.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: RadBERT (pretrained language model) for automated text classification to extract multi-abnormality labels from radiology reports. Llama 3.1 7B for generating question-answer pairs. State-of-the-art 3D nodule segmentation algorithm for extracting nodule information (lobar location, centroid, diameters, and volumes).
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Biases inherent to single-institution dataset may influence self-supervised training. The data originates from a single geographic and clinical setting, which may limit the generalizability of models to other populations.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Dataset originates from single institution limiting generalizability; CT-CLIP depends on specific terminology used in reports and choice of prompts; lack of pretrained 3D medical multimodal AI assistants for benchmarking; models limited to chest CT volumes only; generated reports remain insufficient for clinical use.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: Models remain far from ready for clinical deployment. Challenges such as robustness, interpretability, regulatory compliance, and prospective validation must be addressed before integration into routine radiology workflows. User-friendly graphical interface introduced to broaden accessibility for educational and clinical research settings.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Age (ranging from 18 to 102 years), sex, and geographic location (single institution in Turkey)
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training foundation models for 3D medical imaging, zero-shot multi-abnormality detection, finetuning for classification tasks, visual question-answering, radiology report generation, educational and clinical research settings. Not recommended for clinical deployment without further validation.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: For CT-CHAT training, a visual question-answering (VQA) dataset comprising over 2.7 million question-answer pairs was derived from CT-RATE using Llama 3.1 7B. The dataset consists of several components, including long-answer questions, short-answer questions, multiple-choice questions, and report generation tasks. For report generation enhancement, structured 3D segmentation inputs were integrated by providing detailed nodule information, such as lobar location, centroid, diameters, and volumes, extracted using a state-of-the-art 3D nodule segmentation algorithm on the CT-RATE training set.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: CT-RATE comprises 25,692 non-contrast 3D chest CT volumes reconstructed using various methods to suit different window settings, totaling over 14.3 million 2D slices. Multi-abnormality labels were extracted from radiology reports using an automated text classifier by finetuning a pretrained language model, RadBERT. Within CT-RATE, 1,000 reports were manually annotated for 18 distinct abnormalities for this finetuning procedure. For comparison with 2D models, Digitally Reconstructed Radiographs (DRRs) of 3D chest CT volumes were generated to ensure accurate representation in a 2D context.

rai:dataBiases.evidence: First, biases inherent to our single-institution dataset may influence our self-supervised training. Although we curate a large and diverse set of volume-report pairs, the data originates from a single geographic and clinical setting, which may limit the generalizability of our models to other populations.

rai:dataLimitations.evidence: First, biases inherent to our single-institution dataset may influence our self-supervised training... Second, CT-CLIP depends on the specific terminology used in reports and the choice of prompts during zero-shot detection... Third, the evaluation of CT-CHAT faces limitations due to the lack of pretrained 3D medical multimodal AI assistants for benchmarking... Finally, our current models are limited to chest CT volumes... the quality of its generated reports remains insufficient for clinical use

rai:dataSocialImpact.evidence: That said, it remains far from ready for clinical deployment, as emphasized by our radiologists. As with all AI systems, challenges such as robustness, interpretability, regulatory compliance, and prospective validation must be addressed before integration into routine radiology workflows. To help broaden accessibility, we introduce a user-friendly graphical interface (via our GitHub repository) that allows non-experts to interact with the CT-CHAT model.
